docs.title: Termite Documentation
docs.text: Termite is an AI design assistant for the early design phase. It works inside the CAD tool you already use (Rhino, Revit, Archicad or Grasshopper). You draw a floor boundary, and Termite splits it into units and generates apartment or hotel-room layouts for you.

docs.title: Watch Termite in action
docs.text:
Three short videos, about 5 minutes in total, from an empty model to a finished floor plan.

1. Create a project, floors, staircases and hallwaysRead the steps →

2. Generate a unit mix for each floorRead the steps →

3. Generate a floor planRead the steps →

Shown in Archicad. The steps are the same in Rhino and Revit.

docs.title: How Termite works
docs.text:
There are three steps:

  1. Sign in to the portal. On termite.tools you get your access token, download the plugins and manage your plan.
  2. Install the plugin for your CAD tool and enter your access token.
  3. Design inside your CAD tool. Create a project, define floors, generate a unit mix and then generate floor plans for the units.
Portal  ──►  Plugin (Rhino / Revit / Archicad / Grasshopper)
             │
             └─ Project
                 └─ Floors ──► Unit mix ──► Plan layouts

All your work is saved under a project on the Termite server. You can close your CAD tool and come back to it later.

docs.title: Current version
docs.text:
Plugin version 0.1.0 (first public release) Generative core T_QUEEN_1 Dataset Termite_General

You can always see the generative core and dataset you are using in the Termite bar.

docs.title: The generative core: T_QUEEN_1
docs.text:
T_QUEEN_1 is the AI engine behind Termite. It generates floor plans for residential buildings, mainly apartments.

It was trained on Termite's own internal dataset of 100 architectural plans.

docs.title: What makes it different
docs.text:
Most AI models need very large datasets. T_QUEEN_1 is built to:

  • learn from very little data: a small set of plans is enough to train it
  • handle complex geometry: irregular, angled and non-rectangular boundaries
  • predict shapes it has never seen: it generates good layouts for boundaries that are not in its training data

This means Termite works on your real project shapes, not only on simple rectangles.

docs.title: Engines per plan
docs.text: Plan Engine Server Free General engine (T_QUEEN_1 on the Termite_General dataset) Shared Pro General engine (T_QUEEN_1 on the Termite_General dataset) Shared Enterprise Custom engine trained on your own plans Dedicated server with dedicated resources

docs.title: Shared vs. dedicated
docs.text:
Shared (Free and Pro):

  • Your data stays private. Your projects, floors and plans belong to your account only. Other users cannot see or access them.
  • The engine is the same for everyone. All Free and Pro users use the general T_QUEEN_1 engine. You cannot train it on your own plans.
  • The hardware is shared. Generation runs on servers that all Free and Pro users share. When many people generate at the same time, your results may take a little longer.

Dedicated (Enterprise):

  • Your data is private, just like on the shared server.
  • The server and its resources are yours alone, so no other users affect your speed.
  • The engine can be trained on your own plans.

docs.title: Enterprise: train on your own plans
docs.text:
Because T_QUEEN_1 needs only a small dataset, it can be trained on the plans of your office. Then the generated layouts follow your own design language, standards and typologies.

Enterprise customers get:

  • a dedicated server with dedicated resources
  • a custom engine trained on their own dataset of plans
  • a training service: the Termite team prepares the data, trains the engine and sets it up for you

To discuss an Enterprise setup, contact us at info@termite.tools.

docs.title: Code compliance
docs.text:
Every office works with its own rules: building codes for the region, fire safety distances, and internal standards built up over years. Termite can follow these rules, so the plans it generates fit your regulations and your way of working.

There are three ways to set this up. You can use them on their own or together.

What Termite follows Best for Learn from your drawings Your own plans: sizes, relations, design style Offices with a library of past projects Custom rule dataset Rules we extract from your data: min/max sizes, fire safety distances A default for your office that you can adjust per project Wall types in the settings The wall types you choose for each space Drafting that must match technical standards

docs.title: Learn from your drawings
docs.text:
Send us a set of your own drawings (DWG files of past projects). Termite is trained on them and learns how you design:

  • Sizes: how large you make each type of room
  • Relations: which spaces you put next to each other
  • Design style: the layouts and proportions you prefer
  • Circulation: how you organize hallways, entries and movement through a unit
  • Spatial arrangement: how you place and group the spaces inside a unit

The result is a custom engine trained only on your data and used only by you. Your drawings are never shared or used to train Termite for anyone else. The plans it generates already look like your office's work and fit your workflow, so you spend less time correcting them.

Termite needs only a small set of plans to learn from (see the generative core). Custom engines run on a dedicated server and are part of the Enterprise plan (see engines per plan).

docs.title: Custom rule dataset
docs.text:
You don't need to write your rules down. We extract them from your data for you, and build a custom rule base that Termite follows when it generates plans. For example:

  • the minimum and maximum width of each space
  • the minimum and maximum area of each space
  • fire safety distances, for example the longest allowed distance to an exit

From this rule base we make a default for your office, in the same way as the default of the general Termite dataset (Termite_General). Every new project starts with your default values.

In addition, you can change the default values for each project, depending on:

  • the region and its regulations
  • the context of the site
  • the type of project, for example housing or hotel

When a value changes, the next plans Termite generates follow the new value. You can see the values Termite uses for a project in the dataset program in the Settings tab.

docs.title: Wall types in the settings
docs.text:
Some rules are about how a plan is drafted, not only about its layout. For example, a toilet may need a wall of a certain type and thickness behind it for the plumbing, or your office may have internal standards for the walls around bathrooms or between units.

In the Termite Settings you can choose, per project, which wall types Termite uses: for the exterior walls, the default interior walls, and the walls of each space. When you load a generated plan into your model, Termite draws the walls with these types, so the drafting already follows the regulations you work with.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text: To set up a custom engine or a custom rule dataset for your office, contact us at info@termite.tools. Tell us which regions and project types you work on and which rules matter most to you, and we will prepare the setup with you.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
Termite organizes your work like this:

Project
 └─ Floors
     ├─ Hallways
     ├─ Staircases   (can be shared by several floors)
     └─ Units  ──►  Spaces (bedroom, kitchen, ...)

docs.title: Project
docs.text:
A project is the container for one design. It holds your floors, hallways, staircases, generated units and plans. Everything is saved on the Termite server, so you can open the same project again later.

  • Create a project: in the context bar, next to Project, click + New and type a name.
  • Switch projects: pick another project from the Project dropdown.
  • The plugin remembers the last project you used and opens it next time.

A new project starts with the default list of spaces from the dataset program.

Note

Deleting a project is not available yet.

docs.title: Floor
docs.text:
A floor is a closed outline: the footprint of one level of your building. Termite splits a floor into units.

  • Create a floor: on the Units tab, type a floor name, click Pick Boundary, select a closed polyline and click Send Floor.
  • Pick a floor: use the Floor dropdown in the context bar.
  • Draw it again in CAD: click ⤓ Load next to the Floor dropdown. The floor boundary is drawn into its own layer.
  • Rename or delete a floor from the context bar.

Tip

The boundary must be a closed polyline. Open shapes and true curves (arcs, splines) don't work. See Modeling tips.

docs.title: Hallway
docs.text:
A hallway is a corridor that runs through a floor. Termite keeps hallways free and places units along them.

  • You draw a hallway as a centerline: a line through the middle of the corridor.
  • Each hallway has a name and a width in meters. The default is 1.5 m.
  • A hallway belongs to one floor.

Every floor must have at least one hallway before you generate a unit mix. See Generate a unit mix → Hallways.

docs.title: Staircase
docs.text:
A staircase is a stair or core area that is not part of any unit, for example a stair or an elevator.

  • You draw a staircase as a closed polyline around its footprint.
  • One staircase can run through several floors. The scope sets which floors:
    • Project: every floor in the project
    • Mass: every floor of the current mass
    • Or type specific floor IDs to limit it to those floors.

Every floor must have at least one staircase before you generate a unit mix. See Generate a unit mix → Staircases.

docs.title: Unit
docs.text:
A unit is one part of a floor: an apartment, an office, a shop and so on. Termite creates units for you when you generate a unit mix.

Every unit has a unit type:

Unit type Default area Daylight Residential 40 m² preferred Office 60 m² preferred Retail 80 m² optional Parking 25 m² none Storage 20 m² none

The unit mix is the share of each type on a floor, for example 70% residential and 30% retail.

docs.title: Space
docs.text:
A space is a room inside a unit: a living room, bedroom, kitchen, bathroom and so on. Termite places spaces when you generate a plan for a unit.

Each space has an area, a daylight need (required, preferred, optional or none) and a minimum width. The full list of spaces is the dataset program. You can view it in Settings.

docs.title: Furniture
docs.text:
When you tick Furnished in the Plan tab, Termite adds furniture to the layout it generates. Beds go in the bedrooms, sofas in the living room, a dining table, a kitchen set, and the toilet, washbasin and bath in the bathroom. When you load the plan into your model, the furniture comes with it.

Termite uses one fixed set of standard furniture. Every piece has a real-world size, so a furnished plan also shows you whether the rooms are big enough to live in.

docs.title: Where you get furniture
docs.text: CAD tool Furniture Rhino 2D plan blocks Revit 3D furniture families Archicad 3D objects (Archicad 29)

docs.title: Sizes
docs.text:
Sizes are given as width × depth in centimeters. Width is measured along the front of the piece, depth from back to front.

Beds, sofas, kitchen sets and the other wall pieces stand with their back to a wall. Dining tables stand free in the room.

The pictures below are plan views (seen from above) and use the same scale, so you can compare them with each other.

docs.title: 1. Sign in to the portal
docs.text:
Create an account or sign in at termite.tools. The portal is your account page. It has four tabs:

Tab What it is for Overview Your Termites balance, your access token and your plan Plugins Download the plugins for Rhino, Revit, Archicad and Grasshopper Usage A history of every Termite you received or used Billing Buy more Termites

docs.title: Your access token
docs.text:
The access token connects a plugin to your account. Find it on the Overview tab, then click Show or Copy token.

Keep your token private

Anyone who has your token can use your account. Do not share it or post it online.

docs.title: Termites and plans
docs.text:
Termites are credits. Termite uses them when it generates something, for example a unit mix or a plan layout. The Overview tab shows your balance and the current cost of each action.

  • Every account gets 20 free Termites per month.
  • If you need more, buy a package on the Billing tab (payment through Stripe). Buying Termites also upgrades your account to Pro.
  • The Usage tab lists every action and how many Termites it used.

docs.title: 2. Install a plugin
docs.text:
1. Open the Plugins tab in the portal.
  2. Click Download next to your CAD tool.
  3. Run the installer. When it asks for your access token, paste the token you copied from the Overview tab.
  4. Start your CAD tool. The Termite panel is now available.

Windows warning

Windows may show a "Windows protected your PC" message while you install. Click More info → Run anyway.

docs.title: Where to find Termite in each tool
docs.text:
CAD tool How Termite shows up Rhino A Termite panel inside Rhino Revit A Termite pane inside Revit Archicad A separate Termite app (Start menu or desktop shortcut). It connects to the open Archicad project. Supported versions: Archicad 26–29. Grasshopper A set of Termite components on the canvas. Each step in these docs is one component.

The panel looks and works the same way in Rhino, Revit and Archicad. The screens in these docs use Rhino.

docs.title: 3. The Termite panel
docs.text:
The panel has three parts, from top to bottom:

  1. Termite bar: a collapsible bar with notifications and the Stop, Refresh, Update and Profile buttons. See Settings.
  2. Context bar: three dropdowns that pick what you are working on:
    • Project: the active project
    • Mass: the building mass the floors belong to
    • Floor: the active floor
  3. Tabs:
    • Units: define floors, hallways and staircases, then generate a unit mix. See Generate a unit mix.
    • Plan: generate a floor plan for one unit. See Generate a plan.
    • Settings: the dataset program. See Settings.

Next, read Core concepts.

docs.title: Modeling tips
docs.text: Termite reads geometry straight from your CAD model, so how you draw that geometry affects the result. Read this page before you start a real project.

docs.title: Use polylines, not curves
docs.text:
Termite understands polylines: shapes made of straight segments. It does not understand true curves such as arcs, circles or freeform splines.

This applies to everything you send to Termite: floor boundaries, unit boundaries, hallway centerlines and staircase outlines.

If your design has a curved facade, convert it to a polyline before you send it. For example:

  • Rhino: use Convert (output: lines) or Rebuild to turn a curve into a polyline.
  • Revit: draw the boundary with straight line segments.
  • Archicad: draw the boundary as a Polyline made of straight segments.

docs.title: What to select in each CAD tool
docs.text:
Each input needs a specific type of geometry. If you select the wrong type, Termite shows an error or skips the element.

Input Shape Rhino Revit Archicad Grasshopper Floor boundary (Units tab) Closed outline Closed polyline Floor or Area element, or model/detail lines forming a closed loop Closed Polyline or Slab Closed polyline (boundary input) Hallway (Units tab) Straight centerline Line Model or detail line Line Lines (hallway_curves input) Staircase (Units tab) Closed outline Closed polyline Model or detail lines forming a closed loop Closed Polyline Closed polylines (staircase_curves input) Unit boundary (Plan tab) Closed outline Closed polyline Floor or Area element, or model/detail lines forming a closed loop Closed Polyline or Zone Closed polyline (boundary input) Entry edge (Plan tab) One or more straight edges Line(s) Model or detail line(s) Line(s) or 2-point Polyline(s) Lines Daylight edge (Plan tab) One or more straight edges Line(s) Model or detail line(s) Line(s) or 2-point Polyline(s) Lines (daylights input)

Hallways are straight

Termite uses only the start point and end point of a hallway. If you select a polyline with several segments, Termite sends a straight line between its two ends. Draw an L-shaped or bent corridor as several hallways, one straight line for each segment.

Entry and daylight edges

Draw each edge as a line on top of the matching edge of the unit boundary. In most cases the easiest way is to explode a copy of the unit boundary and keep the segments you need.

docs.title: Edges are used exactly as you draw them
docs.text:
Termite does not simplify or redraw your boundary. Every edge of your polyline is a real edge for Termite. Walls, entries and windows are placed along those edges.

That is why the size of the segments matters:

Your polyline Result Few, reasonably sized edges (for example 1 m or more) Termite can place windows and doors along the edges without problems. Many very small edges (for example a curve split into 10 cm pieces) The edges are too short for windows. Window placement can fail, and the plan can get messy.

Rule of thumb

When you turn a curve into a polyline, use reasonable segment lengths. Make each edge at least long enough to hold a window. Fewer, larger edges give cleaner plans.

The same applies to the entry and daylight edges you select in the Plan tab. Termite can only place a door or a window on an edge that is long enough for it.

docs.title: Levels in Revit and Archicad
docs.text: In Revit and Archicad, every Termite floor is linked to a level (in Archicad: a story).

docs.title: How Termite finds the level
docs.text:
• When you send a floor, Termite reads the level from the elements you selected. For example, a floor or area in Revit, or a slab, zone or polyline in Archicad.
  • If the elements have no level (for example plain lines in Revit), Termite uses the height (Z) of the lines.
  • When you load a plan or units back into your model, Termite puts them on the level at that same height:
    • If a level exists at that height (within 2 mm), Termite uses it.
    • If not, Termite creates a new level at that height.

docs.title: What to watch out for
docs.text:
• Draw on the correct level. Draw or select your boundary in the plan view of the level you want to design. If the boundary is on the wrong level, the results load onto the wrong level.
  • Keep the floor and the view on the same level. In Revit, Termite shows a warning when the active view is on a different level than the selected floor. Hallways and staircases belong to their floor's level, so they won't line up in another view.
  • Archicad: new stories go on top only. Termite can only add a new story above the highest existing story. If it would need a story between two stories or below the lowest, it stops and asks you to create that story in Archicad yourself. That way your existing stories are never moved.
  • Don't change level heights after sending. If you move a level, send the floor again so Termite has the new height.

docs.title: Layers in Rhino
docs.text:
Rhino has no levels, so Termite uses layers instead. The floor name works as the level: every floor gets its own parent layer, and everything Termite draws for that floor goes underneath it.

Level 01                        ← your floor name
 ├─ Floor                       ← the floor boundary
 ├─ Units
 │   ├─ Hallways
 │   └─ Result #12              ← one layer per "Load Units"
 └─ Plan
     └─ Layout_34               ← one layer per "Load in Rhino"
         ├─ Boundaries
         ├─ Walls
         ├─ Doors
         ├─ Windows
         ├─ Tags
         └─ Furniture
Staircases                      ← top level, shared by all floors

Things to know:

  • Staircases have one top-level layer, because one staircase can belong to several floors.
  • Termite creates these layers automatically and sets a default color for each. If you change a layer color, Termite keeps your color.
  • Pick the right floor first. Results are drawn under the floor that is selected in the context bar. If no floor is selected, they go under a layer called Default.
  • Give floors clear names, such as Level 01 or Level 02. The name becomes the layer name.
  • Keep your own drawings (input curves, context, site) on your own layers, not inside Termite's layers. Termite may clear and redraw its layers, for example the Hallways layer when you switch floors.

docs.title: Generate a plan
docs.text:
The Plan tab generates a room layout for one unit: where the bedrooms, kitchen, bathroom and other spaces go.

The tab has two modes. Switch between them with the buttons at the top of the tab:

Mode In short Explore Choose a unit type (for example a two-bedroom apartment). Termite proposes layouts. Sketch Define your own list of rooms and constraints. Coming soon.

docs.title: Explore mode
docs.text:
Use Explore when you want quick layout options for a standard unit type.

Shown in Archicad. The steps are the same in Rhino and Revit. For what to select in your tool, see What to select in each CAD tool.

docs.title: Step 1: Boundary
docs.text:
For the geometry types each CAD tool accepts, see What to select in each CAD tool.

  1. Click Select / Update Boundary. A selection bar opens.
  2. Click Select Unit Boundary and select the closed outline of the unit. This can be a unit from your unit mix or any closed polyline.
  3. Click Select Entry Edge and select the edge where the front door goes.
  4. Click Select Daylight Edge and select the edges on the facade (where windows can go).
  5. Click Finish.

Tip

Termite puts rooms that need daylight, such as living rooms and bedrooms, along the daylight edges. Choose these edges carefully.

docs.title: Step 2: Topology and generate
docs.text:
1. Pick a Category:
    • apartment: studio, one bedroom, two bedrooms, three bedrooms or any
    • hotel-room: one to five beds, or any
  2. Pick a Type from that category. Choose any to let Termite decide.
  3. Options:
    • With loggia: add a loggia (a covered balcony).
    • Furnished: add furniture to the layout.
  4. Threshold: the snapping tolerance Termite uses to clean up the lines of the layout. The default is fine in most cases.
  5. Click Generate Plan.

A progress display shows what Termite is doing. When it is done, the layouts appear as thumbnails.

docs.title: Use the results
docs.text:
Click Load in Rhino (or Load in Revit, and so on) on a tile to draw the plan into your model: walls, rooms and labels, on separate layers.

To get other options, change the type or the boundary edges and generate again.

docs.title: Sketch mode
docs.text:
Coming soon

Sketch mode is not available yet. Use Explore mode for now.

Sketch mode gives you full control over the layout. You will be able to:

  • set your own list of rooms (the topology), with the area of each room and which rooms connect to each other
  • add preferred locations (points that show roughly where a room should be)
  • add fixed geometries (rooms whose shape and position are fixed)
  • add an axis grid that the walls follow

Termite will then generate a plan that follows these inputs.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Termite is in active development. These are the next milestones we are working on, in order.

In development

The features on this page are not available yet. They are planned, and details may change as we build them.

docs.title: 1. Axis grid and columns in planning
docs.text: Termite will take the structure of your building into account when it generates a plan. You will be able to give it the axis grid and the columns, and Termite will place walls and rooms so that they work with the structure: columns stay out of the middle of rooms, and walls follow the grid where it makes sense.

docs.title: 2. Parking planner
docs.text: A planner for parking floors. From the boundary of the floor, the ramps and the cores, Termite will lay out the parking spaces, the driving aisles and the circulation, and help you fit as many spaces as possible.

docs.title: 3. Building mass generation from constraints
docs.text: Termite will generate building masses from the constraints of the site, for example the plot boundary, setbacks, maximum height and the area you need to build. You will get mass options to compare before you start planning the floors and units.

docs.title: 4. Code compliance check agent and final report
docs.text:
An agent that checks a plan against the rules that apply to it: your building codes, fire safety distances and internal standards (see Code compliance). It will point out where a plan does not meet a rule, and produce a final report of the check that you can share with your team or attach to your submission.

Do you have a feature you would like to see in Termite? Tell us at info@termite.tools.

docs.title: Dataset program
docs.text:
The Settings tab shows the dataset program: every space type Termite knows, with its minimum width.

Space Min width (m) living room 3.5 hallway 1.2 dining room 3.0 bedroom 2.5 bathroom 1.5 toilet 0.9 storage 1.0 entry 1.2 kitchen 2.0 laundry 1.5 Loggia 1.5 closet 0.8
  • min_width is the narrowest that space can be in a generated plan.
  • furnitures shows the furniture Termite uses for that space when you generate a furnished plan.

Every new project starts with this list of spaces.

docs.title: The Termite bar
docs.text:
The Termite bar at the top of the panel opens and closes when you click it. It contains:

Item What it does Notifications Messages from Termite, for example when a new version is available ⏹ Stop Stops a generation that is still running ↻ Refresh Reloads projects, floors and results from the server Update Installs a new plugin version when one is available Profile Opens your account in the portal Generative core version The version of the AI model Termite uses Dataset in use The dataset the plans are generated from

docs.title: Access token
docs.text: The plugin stores the access token you entered during installation. To use a new token (for example after you reset it in the portal), install the plugin again and enter the new token.

docs.title: Generate a unit mix
docs.text:
The Units tab splits a floor into units. You give Termite the floor outline, any hallways and staircases, and the mix of unit types you want. Termite returns several options.

Make sure a project is selected in the context bar first. See Core concepts.

Not sure which geometry to select? See What to select in each CAD tool.

The tab has four steps. All four are required: a floor needs a boundary, hallways and staircases before Termite can generate units.

docs.title: Video: project, floors, staircases and hallways
docs.text: Shown in Archicad. The steps are the same in Rhino and Revit. For what to select in your tool, see What to select in each CAD tool.

docs.title: Step 1: Floor boundary
docs.text:
1. Type a Floor Name, for example Level 01. If you leave it empty, Termite names it Floor 1, Floor 2 and so on.
  2. Click Pick Boundary and select the closed polyline of the floor in your model.
  3. Click Send Floor.

The new floor appears in the Floor dropdown and is selected.

Note

If a floor with the same name already exists, Termite asks whether to update it.

docs.title: Step 2: Hallways
docs.text:
Required

Every floor needs at least one hallway. Termite places the units along the hallways.

  1. Click Select Centerlines and select one or more lines that run through the middle of your corridors.
  2. Every hallway appears as a row. Change its name and width if needed.
  3. Click Submit.

Row buttons:

  • Remove: removes the row from this list only. The saved hallway stays on the server.
  • Delete: deletes the hallway permanently.
  • ↻ Refresh: reloads the saved hallways for the current floor.

docs.title: Step 3: Staircases
docs.text:
Required

Every floor needs at least one staircase. Termite uses it as the escape route for the fire safety distance.

  1. Choose the Scope:
    • Mass: the staircase is on every floor of the current mass.
    • Project: the staircase is on every floor of the project.
  2. Click Select Staircase Regions and select one closed polyline for each staircase.
  3. To limit a staircase to certain floors, type their IDs in Floors (ids, blank = all).
  4. Click Submit.

Remove, Delete and ↻ Refresh work the same way as for hallways.

docs.title: Step 4: Preferences and generate
docs.text: Shown in Archicad. The steps are the same in Rhino and Revit. For what to select in your tool, see What to select in each CAD tool.

docs.title: Unit mix table
docs.text:
Add one row for each unit type you want:

Column Meaning Name The unit type, for example Residential or Office Percentage % The share of the floor for this type Area The target area of one unit, in m²

Warning

The percentages must add up to 100%. If they don't, Termite shows a warning and does not generate.

Example: 80% Residential at 45 m² and 20% Retail at 80 m².

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: Setting Default Meaning Min unit width (m) 3.5 No unit is narrower than this Fire safety distance (m) 15 The maximum distance from a unit to an escape route

docs.title: Advanced (optional)
docs.text:
Click ▸ Advanced to fine-tune the generator. The defaults work well for most cases.

Setting Default Meaning Number of Results 3 How many options you get (1–10) Exploration per Iteration 10% How much each round tries new ideas. Higher means more variety. Iterations 100 How long Termite searches (50–250). More iterations give better results but take longer.

docs.title: Generate
docs.text: Click Generate Units. The status line shows the progress. When the run is done, the results appear as thumbnails.

docs.title: Use the results

• Every result is a tile named Result #….
  • Click Load Units on a tile to draw that result into your model. Each unit gets its own outline and a label (Unit 1, Unit 2, …).
  • To try other options, change the mix or the constraints and generate again.

Next: pick a unit and generate a plan for it.
